page: Amazon Web Services m8id.2xlarge is a general-purpose instance powered by the Nitro hypervisor and an Intel Xeon 6975P-C processor. This x86_64 architecture server features 8 dedicated vCPUs across 4 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled, running at a clock speed of 3.9 GHz. The processor includes a 480 MB L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512 and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) for vector and matrix operations. The instance is equipped with 32.0 GB of DDR5 memory operating at 7 GHz, providing 4.0 GB of memory per core. Local storage is provided via a bundled 474 GB NVMe SSD instance store volume, and baseline network bandwidth is rated at 4 Gbps.

Benchmark results indicate strong performance in specific single-threaded workloads. The instance achieves top-tier status in Geekbench text processing with a score of 2981.0 and demonstrates strong performance in single-threaded gzip compression at 34.23 GB/sec and single-threaded bzip3 decompression at 14.58 GB/sec. Geekbench single-core testing yields a score of 2207.0, which is also in the strong tier. Multi-core and general computational benchmarks, including a stress-ng multi-core score of 8647.23 and a PassMark CPU score of 15614.47, fall within the average range. Memory bandwidth tests show an average read-only small block cached speed of 643.45 GB/sec, while uncached large block read and write speeds are 71.09 GB/sec and 52.95 GB/sec respectively.

With its balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio and integrated NVMe SSD storage, the m8id.2xlarge is designed for general-purpose workloads that require fast local scratch space. It is suitable for database operations, web serving, and software compilation, as evidenced by its average PassMark database score of 5057.49 and static web serving throughput of 15.52 GB/sec. The inclusion of AMX instructions supports small-scale machine learning tasks, with the instance achieving a strong text generation speed of 278.18 tokens/sec on a 135M parameter model. The bundled local NVMe storage provides qualitative cost efficiency for applications that would otherwise require provisioned block storage, though the lack of complimentary public IPv4 addresses should be factored into deployment planning.
